lesson.body:
Think of a grape like a tomato ripening in the sun. In a cooler place — a foggy coast, or a marginal region like Champagne or Chablis — grapes ripen slowly over a long, mild season. By harvest they hold more acidity (the tart, zingy quality that makes your mouth water) — warmth burns acid off faster, and these grapes never got that hot — and they build up less sugar. Less sugar at picking means less for yeast to turn into alcohol, so the wine ends up lighter and lower in alcohol, with crisp, tart, sometimes herbal flavours, like a green apple.

In a warmer place — sun-soaked Spain, Australia, or much of California — grapes ripen fast and pack in more sugar, which ferments into more alcohol, while their acidity fades in the heat. These wines feel fuller and rounder (that weight is called "body," like cream versus skim milk), with sweet, jammy, ripe-fruit flavours, like a sun-warmed plum.

The fun part: the same grape can become two different wines depending on where it grew. Climate sets the stage, though the winemaker's choices — like when to pick — shape the final style too.
outcomes: Explain how climate changes a grape's acidity and sugar
Tell cool-climate and warm-climate wine styles apart
Predict a wine's style from where its grapes grew

steps.title: Cool climates keep grapes tart and zingy

steps.q: What do cool-climate grapes hold more of at harvest?
steps.why: A long, mild season keeps acidity high. Warmth burns acid off, and these grapes never got that hot.

steps.body: Cool-climate grapes also build up less sugar. Yeast turns sugar into alcohol, so less sugar at picking means a lighter wine, lower in alcohol. Expect crisp, tart, sometimes herbal flavours.
steps.tip: Picture biting into a green apple: crisp and tart. That's the classic cool-climate taste.
steps.title: Less sugar means lighter, lower-alcohol wine

steps.q: Which words can describe a cool-climate wine?
steps.why: Cool-climate wines taste crisp and tart, sometimes herbal. Jammy flavours belong to wines from warm places.

steps.q: Cool-climate wines tend to be lower in alcohol because the grapes built up less sugar.
steps.why: Yeast turns sugar into alcohol. Less sugar at picking leaves less to turn into alcohol.

steps.body: In sun-soaked Spain, Australia or much of California, grapes ripen fast. They pack in more sugar, which ferments into more alcohol, while acidity fades in the heat. The wines feel fuller and rounder, with jammy, ripe-fruit flavours.

steps.title: Warm sun makes riper, fuller wines

steps.q: A grape grows in sun-soaked Australia. What is its wine likely to be like?
steps.why: Heat ripens grapes fast and packs in sugar, which ferments into more alcohol. The wine feels fuller.

steps.q: In a warm climate, grapes hold on to more of their acidity.
steps.why: Acidity fades in the heat. Cool-climate grapes keep more of it, which is why their wines taste crisp.

lesson.summary: The climate where grapes grow shapes a wine's style — cooler regions make lighter, tarter, lower-alcohol wines, while warmer regions make fuller, riper, higher-alcohol ones, even from the very same grape.
lesson.title: Cool-climate vs warm-climate wines

bank.q: Acidity is the tart, zingy part of a wine. What does it do in your mouth?
bank.why: Acidity is the zing that makes your mouth water. The more acid, the more you salivate.

bank.q: Which of these does the lesson name as cool places to grow grapes?
bank.why: A foggy coast, Champagne and Chablis all ripen grapes slowly over a long, mild season. A baking-hot valley is the opposite.

bank.why: Cool-climate grapes ripen slowly over a long, mild season, and that is how they keep their acidity.

bank.why: Crisp and tart, like biting into a green apple. That is the classic cool-climate flavour.

bank.q: Grapes A were picked with lots of sugar, grapes B with much less. Which usually gives the lighter, lower-alcohol wine?
bank.why: Yeast turns sugar into alcohol. Less sugar in grapes B leaves less to turn into alcohol, so the wine is lighter.

bank.q: In winemaking, yeast turns the grapes' acidity into alcohol.
bank.why: Yeast feeds on sugar, not acid. That is why grapes picked with less sugar give a lighter wine, lower in alcohol.

bank.q: Which of these usually happen to grapes in a hot, sunny climate?
bank.why: Heat ripens grapes fast, so they build up more sugar while their acidity fades.

bank.q: What is the wine word for how full and heavy a wine feels in your mouth?
bank.why: That weight is called body. Think of cream versus skimmed milk.

bank.q: Which of these places does the lesson describe as warm and sunny?
bank.why: Sun-soaked Spain is a warm place. Chablis, Champagne and foggy coasts are the lesson's cool examples.

bank.q: Where a grape grows can change the style of wine it makes.
bank.why: The same grape can give two very different wines, depending on whether it grew somewhere cool or warm.

bank.q: One grape is grown in a cool spot and a warm spot. Which of these fit the warm-spot wine?
bank.why: Warmth gives riper grapes with more sugar, so the wine is fuller and stronger. Sharp acidity and green apple point to the cool spot.

bank.q: A winemaker in a warm region wants a fresher, lighter wine. Which choice could help?
bank.why: Grapes gain sugar and lose acidity as they ripen. Picking earlier keeps more freshness and gives less alcohol.

deep_notes: Grapes carry two main acids: tartaric acid, and malic acid, the sharp acid also found in green apples. As grapes ripen, the grapes use up some of their malic acid, and it does so faster when it is warm, especially on warm nights. That is why growers love cool nights. Pros call the gap between day and night temperatures the diurnal range: warm days build ripeness, cool nights keep freshness.

As a rough rule, yeast needs about 17 grams of sugar per litre of juice to make 1% alcohol, so small changes in ripeness show up on the label. When grapes struggle to ripen, some cool regions, such as Burgundy and Champagne, allow winemakers to add sugar before or during fermentation. This raises the alcohol without making the wine sweet. It is called chaptalisation, after the French minister Jean-Antoine Chaptal.

In hot places the problem flips. Sugar races ahead while acidity drops, and a wine with too little acidity tastes flat, which pros call flabby. Winemakers in many warm regions, including Australia and California, are allowed to add acid, usually tartaric acid, to bring back freshness. A ripe Barossa Valley Shiraz from South Australia often reaches 14.5% alcohol or more.

A classic pair is Syrah. From the northern Rhône in France, which is much cooler than South Australia's Barossa Valley, it often tastes of blackberry and black pepper, with fresh acidity. From the warm Barossa, where it is called Shiraz, it turns riper and fuller, with jammy black fruit and hints of chocolate. Winemakers can also work against their climate: picking early in a warm place keeps more acidity and less alcohol.

deeper.body: Most of the world's vineyards sit between about 30 and 50 degrees of latitude, north and south of the equator. Nearer the equator it is usually too hot. Nearer the poles it is too cold. Champagne lies close to 49 degrees north, near the cool edge, which is why its grapes stay so high in acid. Southern England, just beyond 50 degrees, now makes fine sparkling wine too.
deeper.title: The vine belt

deeper.q: Why do Champagne's grapes keep so much acidity?
deeper.why: At about 49 degrees north, Champagne is close to the cool limit for grapes, so they ripen slowly and keep their acid.

deeper.body: Pros also sort climates by what surrounds them. A maritime climate lies near the sea, which keeps temperatures mild, with small gaps between summer and winter. Bordeaux is the classic case. A continental climate lies far inland, with hot summers, cold winters and a real risk of spring frost. Burgundy leans this way. The sea brings rain too, so maritime vineyards often battle rot, a mould that spoils the grapes.
deeper.title: Maritime or continental

deeper.q: A continental climate has smaller swings between summer and winter than a maritime one.
deeper.why: It is the reverse. Inland, continental places get hot summers and cold winters, while the sea keeps maritime places mild.

deeper.body: Ripeness is not only about sugar. Pros also talk about phenolic ripeness: whether the flavours and tannins (the drying grip on your gums) in the skins and seeds have matured. In a hot place, sugar can race ahead before the flavours catch up. Waiting gives a very strong wine, while picking early gives green, harsh flavours. So many growers walk the rows, chew the grapes and check that the seeds have turned brown.
deeper.title: Ripe is not just sweet

deeper.q: Which of these does a grower check to judge phenolic ripeness?
deeper.why: Phenolic ripeness is about skins and seeds maturing. Brown seeds and ripe-tasting skins show the grapes are truly ready.

v2.body:
In 1988 an American couple, Stuart and Sandy Moss, planted Champagne's grapes (Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier) at **Nyetimber** in West Sussex, where most English growers chose hardy German-bred grapes. Their first wine, from the 1992 harvest, won a trophy at the International Wine and Spirit Competition. England, at about 51 degrees north, could ripen Champagne's grapes.

That story is about **climate**: a region's long-run average warmth, usually worked out from about 30 years of weather. One hot summer does not make a cool region warm. Terroir is a site's fixed features, like soil and slope; the vintage, one year's weather against the average. Measured in degrees from the equator, most of the world's vineyards lie in a **vine belt** between about 30 and 50 degrees north and south. Nearer the equator it is usually too hot for fine wine grapes, nearer the poles too cold. Champagne, at about 49 degrees north, sits near the cool edge.

Grapes gain sugar and lose acidity (sourness) as they ripen, faster in heat. Cool places make lighter, tarter, lower-alcohol wines with green apple and citrus fruit. Warm places make fuller, softer, stronger wines with ripe, dark, jammy fruit.

A **marginal climate** sits at the cool edge, where grapes only just ripen in an average year: England, Champagne, the Mosel. A cold year can leave them sour, yet some of the most prized wines grow there. Through Burgundy and Bordeaux it warms, and hot regions such as the Barossa ripen grapes every year.

Growers work with their climate: they plant early ripeners such as Pinot Noir in cool places and heat lovers such as Grenache in hot ones. In warm regions they pick earlier, keeping acidity and lowering alcohol, or seek cooler sites. Higher up it is about 0.6°C cooler per 100 metres, and cool nights after hot days help grapes keep acidity; near the sea, cool breezes help. In a cool year winemakers may use **chaptalisation**: adding sugar to the juice so the yeast makes more alcohol, not a sweeter wine. Burgundy and Champagne allow it; California bans it. Warm regions add acid instead.

The **alcohol** on a label is a clue: 14.5% or more suggests heat or very ripe grapes (Barossa Shiraz), about 13% sits in between, and about 12% suggests a cool place or early picking (Chablis). Under 10% often means a cool wine that kept some sweetness, like a Mosel Kabinett. Added sugar can lift the figure.

The map is moving; warmer summers are part of the reason. The Torres family has planted at about 950 metres in the Pyrenees foothills, the Champagne house Taittinger has planted in Kent, and Bordeaux now allows a few **heat-tolerant grapes**. The UK now has over 1,000 vineyards; most of its wine is sparkling.
deep_notes: Modern English wine is young. Its revival is usually dated to the early 1950s, when Major General Sir Guy Salisbury-Jones planted vines at Hambledon, in Hampshire. For decades most growers chose early-ripening German-bred grapes such as Müller-Thurgau and the hardy hybrid Seyval Blanc, and many of the still wines were thin and tart. Nyetimber is usually named as the first English estate to plant only Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier for sparkling wine. Others, Hambledon among them, later turned to the same three grapes.

Weather services work with 30-year averages, which the World Meteorological Organization calls climate normals; the current set covers 1991 to 2020. Because the window rolls forward, a region's normal can drift, one way to see the moving map at the end of this lesson. Averages also hide the spread: two regions with the same average warmth can differ in how often a cold year strikes, and that spread is what the next lesson's vintages are about.

The southern band takes in the vineyards of Chile, Argentina, South Africa, Australia and all of New Zealand, whose Central Otago lies at about 45 degrees south. Latitude sets day length and how high the sun climbs, but it is only a starting point. Cold sea currents, coastal fog and altitude can make a place far cooler than its latitude suggests.

Small changes in ripeness show up on the label. Each 1% of alcohol takes about 17 grams of sugar per litre of juice, so juice with around 200 grams of sugar per litre can ferment to about 12%, and riper juice to 14% or more. Flavour follows warmth too: the same grape tends to move from green apple and citrus in a cool place towards ripe, dark or tropical fruit in a hot one.

Marginal regions are where the weather of each year matters most, because there is little margin for a cool, wet summer. That is one reason vintages vary more in Champagne or the Mosel than in a hot region, a story the next lesson picks up. The prize for living at the edge is a long, slow ripening season, which lets flavour build while the grapes keep the fresh acidity that makes Champagne, Mosel Riesling and red Burgundy so prized.

Each grape needs a certain amount of warmth to ripen. Pinot Noir and Chardonnay ripen early, which is why they are the grapes of Burgundy, Champagne and England. Cabernet Sauvignon ripens late, so in Bordeaux it does best on warm gravel. Grenache needs a long, hot, dry season and thrives in the southern Rhône and Spain. Picking date is a style choice too: sparkling wine growers pick early on purpose, for sharp, low-alcohol base wine.

Jean-Antoine Chaptal was a chemist who served as Napoleon's Minister of the Interior from 1800 to 1804. In his 1801 book on making wine he recommended adding sugar to the juice of underripe grapes to make a stronger, longer-lasting wine. The idea was older, but his name stuck. In Germany, Qualitätswein may be chaptalised while Prädikatswein may not. California allows grape concentrate instead of sugar.

The alcohol figure works best as one clue among several, and the grape matters as much as the place. Some grapes pile up sugar easily: Grenache and Zinfandel can easily reach 15% or more, so a high figure on those labels says as much about the grape as the climate. Winemakers in warm places can also pick early for a lighter style. So read the number with the place and the grape. A Mosel Riesling at 8% and a Barossa Shiraz at 15% tell very different climate stories.

Taittinger bought farmland near Chilham, in Kent, in 2015 and planted Chardonnay, Pinot Noir and Pinot Meunier there in 2017, often described as the first big Champagne house to set up a vineyard in England. In Catalonia, Miguel A. Torres began planting near Tremp in 1998, at about 950 metres, on high ground the family now treats as part of its answer to a warming climate. Bordeaux's newcomers, such as Marselan and Touriga Nacional, may make up only a small part of a blend.

deeper.body: Climate scientists such as Gregory Jones sum up a region's warmth with one figure: the average temperature over the growing season, April to October in the north and October to April in the south. Most quality wine regions fall between roughly 13 and 21°C (some studies say 12 and 22°C). Pinot Noir sits near the cool end; Grenache and Zinfandel need more warmth, higher up. It is a simpler cousin of the Winkler degree-days drawn up in California.
deeper.title: One number for a region's warmth

deeper.key: The growing season average: April to October in the north, October to April in the south.
opts: The hottest single day of the year
The temperature of the soil in winter
The heat of the fermenting juice
deeper.q: What does a region's growing season temperature measure?
deeper.remember: One season, one average, one climate clue.
deeper.why: One average lets you compare regions: most quality wine regions sit between roughly 13 and 21°C.

deeper.body: EU law divides vineyards into climate zones and limits how far adding sugar may raise the alcohol: 3% in the coolest zone, 2% in the next and 1.5% in the warmest. In exceptionally poor years the cap can rise by up to 0.5%. In Italy, Spain, Portugal, Greece and Cyprus, ordinary sugar is not allowed at all: winemakers who need more strength must use concentrated grape must, juice with much of its water removed.
deeper.title: Europe rations the sugar

deeper.key: The EU limit on raising alcohol is highest in the coolest zone, 3%, and lower in warmer zones.
deeper.q: Under EU rules, winemakers in the coolest zones may raise alcohol by adding sugar more than those in warmer zones.
deeper.why: Cool zones struggle most to ripen grapes, so they get the most room to correct.

deeper.body: Chaptalisation and acidification answer opposite problems. Underripe grapes from a cool year are short of sugar and rich in acid; overripe grapes from a hot one carry plenty of sugar but too little acid. So EU rules treat adding sugar and adding acid to the same wine as mutually exclusive, allowing exceptions only by special decision. A winemaker who needs both has usually picked at the wrong moment, which is why the picking date matters so much.
deeper.title: Sugar or acid, but rarely both

deeper.key: Sugar fixes underripe grapes and acid fixes overripe ones, so EU rules normally allow only one per wine.
opts: Sugar and acid react to make gas
Both are banned outright in the EU
Acid stops the yeast from working
deeper.q: Why do EU rules normally forbid adding both sugar and acid to the same wine?
deeper.remember: Short of sugar or short of acid: pick one.
deeper.why: The two fixes answer opposite problems, so needing both usually points to a badly timed harvest.

steps.body: Warmer summers are part of the reason. Places once thought too cold now ripen grapes, and warm regions climb higher or change grapes. The UK now has over 1,000 vineyards, and most of its wine is sparkling.

items.label: Towards the poles
items.text: The Champagne house Taittinger has planted vines in Kent, in England.

items.label: Uphill
items.text: The Spanish Torres family planted at about 950 metres in the Pyrenees.

items.label: New grapes
items.text: Bordeaux now allows a few grapes that cope better with heat.

steps.tip: An English sparkling wine on the shelf is a small sign of a warming map.
steps.title: Vineyards are creeping towards the poles, and uphill

steps.key: Chaptalisation adds sugar to the juice so the yeast makes more alcohol, not a sweeter wine.
opts: Adds acid to freshen the wine
Adds sugar to make it sweeter
Adds sugar to lift the alcohol
steps.remember: Chaptalisation feeds the yeast, not your sweet tooth.
steps.why: It helps cool regions such as Burgundy and Champagne in years when grapes struggle to ripen.

steps.key: An earlier harvest in a warm region keeps acidity and lowers alcohol.
steps.q: A Barossa grower wants a fresher, lighter Shiraz. Picking earlier would help.
steps.remember: Pick early for fresh, pick late for strong.
steps.why: Grapes gain sugar and lose acidity as they ripen, so the picking date shapes the style.

steps.key: 14.5% or more suggests heat or very ripe grapes, as in Barossa Shiraz.
opts: A hot climate or very ripe grapes
A wine that kept its sugar
steps.q: A red wine's label says 15% alcohol. What does that most likely suggest?
steps.why: More sugar in riper grapes means more alcohol, so a high figure hints at a warm climate.

cards.back: A region's long-run average warmth. One year's weather against that average is the vintage.
The bands between about 30 and 50 degrees north and south where most vineyards grow.
A cool-edge region, like England or Champagne, where grapes only just ripen in an average year.
Adding sugar to the juice so the yeast makes more alcohol, not a sweeter wine.
